title: Authentication Methods
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 5: Identity and Access Management (IAM): Authentication Methods.

items: Type 1 — Something You Know — Password, PIN, security question
Type 2 — Something You Have — Smart card, token, phone
Type 3 — Something You Are — Biometrics (fingerprint, iris, face)
Type 4 — Somewhere You Are — Geolocation, IP address
Type 5 — Something You Do — Behavioral biometrics (typing pattern, gait)

blocks.text: From Chapple: "The three factors of authentication are something you know (such as a password or PIN), something you have (such as a smartcard or token), and something you are (based on biometrics). Multifactor authentication includes two or more authentication factors, and using it is more secure than using a single factor." ⚠️ Exam Trap: The classic three factors are Types 1-3. Types 4 and 5 are supplementary. MFA requires factors from at LEAST two DIFFERENT categories. Two passwords = single factor (both are Type 1).

items: Combines two or more DIFFERENT authentication factor types
Much stronger than any single factor alone
Required by many compliance frameworks (PCI DSS, HIPAA)
Two-factor (2FA) — minimum acceptable MFA
All factors should be independent — compromise of one shouldn't reveal another
Password (Type 1) + Hardware token (Type 2) = 2FA
PIN (Type 1) + Fingerprint (Type 3) = 2FA
Smart card (Type 2) + PIN (Type 1) = 2FA
Password + Security question = Single factor (both Type 1)
Two different PINs = Single factor (both Type 1)

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: SMS-based MFA (receiving codes via text) is weaker than app-based or hardware tokens because SMS can be intercepted (SIM swapping, SS7 attacks). However, SMS MFA is still better than no MFA.

items: Complexity — Require uppercase, lowercase, numbers, special characters
Length — Minimum 8-12 characters (longer is better)
History — Prevent reuse of recent passwords (typically last 12-24)
Aging — Force periodic changes (debated; NIST now recommends against forced rotation)
Account lockout — Lock after failed attempts (typically 3-5)
Favor longer passwords/passphrases over complexity rules
Don't force periodic password changes (unless breach suspected)
Screen passwords against known compromised password lists
Allow paste into password fields (encourages password managers)
Don't use password hints or knowledge-based questions
Never store passwords in plaintext
Use salted hashes (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2)
Salt = random value added before hashing to prevent rainbow table attacks

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: NIST's updated guidance RECOMMENDS AGAINST forced periodic password changes. However, the CISSP exam may still test traditional password policies. Know both perspectives.

items: Physiological — Fingerprint, iris, retina, facial recognition, palm vein
Behavioral — Voice pattern, typing rhythm, signature dynamics, gait
Crossover Error Rate (CER/EER) — Where FAR and FRR meet; lower = better accuracy
False Accept Rate (FAR/Type II) — Unauthorized person accepted (security risk)
False Reject Rate (FRR/Type I) — Authorized person rejected (usability issue)

blocks.text: Biometric Ranking by Accuracy: Iris > Retina > Fingerprint > Palm > Voice > Face > Signature From Shon Harris: Biometric factors include "something you are (based on biometrics)." Side channel attacks can target biometric systems "by gathering data pertaining to how a device operates." ⚠️ Exam Trap: FAR (Type II error) is MORE DANGEROUS than FRR (Type I error). FAR lets unauthorized users in. FRR merely inconveniences legitimate users. To increase security, lower the FAR (which increases FRR — tradeoff). ⚠️ Exam Trap: Retina scans are the MOST accurate but also the MOST invasive. They can reveal health conditions, raising privacy concerns.

items: Hardware tokens — Physical devices generating one-time codes (RSA SecurID)
Software tokens — Apps generating TOTP codes (Google Authenticator)
Smart cards — Contain embedded certificate/key (CAC, PIV)
HOTP — HMAC-based One-Time Password (counter-based)
TOTP — Time-based One-Time Password (time-based; most common)

blocks.text: From Shon Harris: Smart cards "require physical interaction with a reader (contact) or no physical interaction with the reader (contactless architectures). Two contactless architectures are combi (one chip) and hybrid (two chips)." Smart Card Components:

items: Embedded microprocessor or memory chip
Stores X.509 certificates and private keys
Requires PIN to unlock (two-factor: something you have + something you know)
Resistant to cloning when using crypto processor
